terms.definition: The output produced per unit of input, such as per worker or per hour.
terms.whyItMatters: Higher productivity lowers cost and builds competitive advantage.

terms.definition: Successive stages of a channel run as one coordinated unit instead of independent bargainers, in exactly three forms: corporate, where a single owner holds title at every stage; contractual, where legally separate firms are bound by agreement such as a franchise or retailer cooperative; and administered, where neither ownership nor contract exists and one member's sheer size dictates terms.
terms.whyItMatters: Marketing and channel exams show a scenario and ask which of the three forms it is; the corporate/contractual line is ownership, and the contractual/administered line is whether a signed agreement exists.

terms.definition: Two-part credential in financial planning, analysis and strategic decision support, requiring a bachelor's degree, two years of management-accounting experience, and 30 continuing hours a year of which 2 must be ethics. It is built for internal decision support, whereas the CPA license exists for the external attest work a CMA holder may not sign.
terms.whyItMatters: A corporate-finance roleplay asking which credential fits a cost-analyst career path needs this internal-versus-external split stated with its hour requirement.

terms.definition: Production and consumption happen at the same instant with the buyer present, so the employee is part of the product and no defective unit can be caught before a customer receives it; a manufactured good is built, inspected, and warehoused weeks before anyone buys it.
terms.whyItMatters: Service-quality roleplays are scored on front-line hiring and training as quality control, because there is no inspection step to add between production and the customer.

terms.definition: The slice of the serviceable available market a company expects to capture within the plan horizon: SAM times a realistic share percentage, so a $200 million SAM at 4% share is an $8 million target. Unlike SAM it is a forecast the plan is held to, not a ceiling.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the number a judge compares against the plan's revenue projection and marketing budget; a SOM larger than the funded plan can deliver is the fastest way to lose credibility in a presentation.

terms.definition: A structured pitch showing how an offering meets the customer's needs.
terms.whyItMatters: A compelling presentation moves a prospect toward purchase.

terms.definition: The share of each ADDITIONAL dollar of after-tax income a household spends rather than saves, computed as the change in consumption divided by the change in income. It always pairs with the marginal propensity to save, and the two sum to 1 — so an MPC of 0.75 implies an MPS of 0.25.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that give a household's income increase and its spending increase want this ratio, which then feeds the spending multiplier; using average spending out of total income instead of the change is the classic error.

terms.definition: A lump sum a supplier pays a retail chain to get a new item onto the shelf and into the item file, commonly $250 to $25,000 per SKU per chain, charged before a single unit sells and rarely refunded if the item fails. It buys placement, whereas a promotional allowance pays for advertising or display the retailer actually performs and can be documented.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics questions in channel management use it to ask whether the practice locks small suppliers out of shelf space, and product-launch roleplays must budget it as a sunk cost of entry.

terms.definition: A director's legal obligation to inform themselves of reasonably available material facts before deciding — the diligence half of board duty — as opposed to the duty of loyalty, which forbids self-dealing and requires putting the corporation's interest ahead of personal gain.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-law exam items describe a director who approved a merger without reading the valuation report and expect the specific duty breached to be named.

terms.definition: The liability booked at the moment of sale for repairs expected later -- units sold times expected claim rate times cost per claim, so 100,000 units at a 2% claim rate and $40 per claim accrues $80,000 of expense in the period the revenue is recognized, not when the repairs happen.
terms.whyItMatters: Questions pairing a generous warranty with its cost are answered with this accrual; a roleplay proposing a longer warranty has to price it, and the reserve is the number to quote.

terms.definition: An assessment of internal and external factors affecting a business's marketing.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding the situation must come before any recommendation.

terms.definition: A higher commission rate applied only to revenue above quota — 8% up to plan and 12% beyond it — so each dollar of overperformance pays more than the first dollar did. A cap or a decelerator does the reverse and is precisely what tempts a rep to hold a signed deal until the next period opens.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items on motivating a sales force ask which plan change stops sandbagging at quarter end, and the rate structure above quota is the mechanism being tested.

terms.definition: Equals 1 divided by (1 − MPC), so an economy whose households spend 80 cents of each extra dollar turns $10 billion of new government purchases into as much as $50 billion of added output. The tax multiplier is always smaller, because the first dollar of a tax cut is partly saved before any of it is spent.
terms.whyItMatters: A macro item that supplies an MPC and a spending figure is asking for this computation; the tax-cut version of the same question uses a smaller multiplier and is where competitors lose points.

terms.definition: Cutting an existing layer out of a channel so the producer reaches the buyer directly — a manufacturer closing its distributor network and selling from its own site. Its mirror image, reintermediation, is a NEW intermediary re-entering that same direct channel, such as a marketplace or comparison platform that resells the manufacturer's goods after the old distributor was removed.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about launching direct-to-consumer are scored on whether you flag the dealer backlash and the fact that the removed layer's functions still have to be performed by somebody.

terms.definition: Ranks a customer file on three purchase behaviors, how recently they bought, how often they buy and how much they have spent in total, scoring each into quintiles from 1 to 5 so that a 555 is the strongest target and a 155 flags a heavy spender who has gone quiet; it segments on recorded transactions rather than on demographics.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked which customers should get a reactivation offer, this produces a defensible list straight from the database instead of a guess about who looks likely.

terms.definition: Unused capacity is destroyed the moment it goes unsold: a 200-room hotel that sells 150 rooms tonight cannot add the other 50 to tomorrow's inventory, which is why capacity is priced by demand period; unsold physical goods simply stay in inventory and sell later.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about slow midweek nights are scored on demand-shifting tactics -- off-peak pricing, overbooking policy -- that follow directly from capacity that cannot be stored.

terms.definition: One percentage point of category share, worth 1% of total industry sales in dollars — $40 million in a $4 billion category. Moving from 10% to 11% share is one point but an 11% relative gain, and plans state objectives in points precisely to keep the two apart.
terms.whyItMatters: Objective-setting items ask what a stated share gain is worth in revenue, which requires multiplying the point value by industry sales rather than by the company's own sales.

terms.definition: Responding to a customer's concerns in a helpful, persuasive way.
terms.whyItMatters: Handling objections improves trust and conversion.

terms.definition: Totals a nation's output as C + I + G + (X − M) — consumption plus business investment plus government purchases plus net exports. Imports are SUBTRACTED because they were produced abroad but already counted inside C, I and G, which is why a widening trade deficit mechanically lowers the measured figure.
terms.whyItMatters: GDP items hand you four spending categories and expect the sum with imports netted out; adding imports in, or counting government transfer payments as G, are the two ways competitors miss it.

terms.definition: Money taken off the invoice for a channel FUNCTION the reseller performs — buying a truckload, stocking ahead of season, or warehousing the goods. A promotional allowance pays instead for ADVERTISING or display effort. Both fall under Robinson-Patman sections 2(d) and 2(e), which require that they be offered on proportionally equal terms to every competing reseller, so a deal given only to the largest chain is the violation.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a big-box buyer demands a deal the independents will not get is scored on citing the proportionally-equal-terms requirement rather than on negotiating skill.

terms.term: Gross margin return on inventory investment (GMROI)
terms.definition: Ties margin to the money tied up in stock: gross margin dollars / average inventory at cost, which equals gross-margin percent multiplied by the sales-to-stock ratio. A result of 3.00 means three dollars of margin per dollar invested, whereas inventory turnover counts how often stock sells and says nothing about the margin earned each turn.
terms.whyItMatters: A buyer's roleplay compares two vendors with identical turnover and different margins, and this is the single figure that separates them for the judge.

terms.definition: Defect count divided by units shipped, times 1,000,000: 35 rejects out of 500,000 units is 70, the scale supplier scorecards use because the same figure written as a percentage -- 0.007% -- rounds toward nothing and cannot separate a good supplier from an excellent one.
terms.whyItMatters: Vendor-selection roleplays hand you competing quality records; comparing them on this scale, rather than on a rounded percentage, is what makes the recommendation defensible.

terms.definition: The share of industry unit volume a plan must win just to cover its fixed costs: fixed costs / contribution margin per unit gives break-even units, then those units / total industry units. $2,000,000 of fixed cost at $10 contribution needs 200,000 units, which is 5% of a 4-million-unit category.
terms.whyItMatters: New-product plans are judged on whether the required share is plausible against the shares incumbents already hold; a break-even share above the category leader's is a plan a judge will reject on sight.

terms.definition: Sizing territories by the work each contains: accounts multiplied by the calls per year each requires, divided by the calls one rep can make — 400 accounts needing 12 calls each is 4,800 calls, and at 800 calls per rep that is six territories. The breakdown method instead divides a sales forecast by average revenue per rep and ignores how much service each account demands.
terms.whyItMatters: A management roleplay asking you to rebalance territories after a merger wants the calculation and the service load, not an even split of the map.

terms.definition: A general, ongoing rise in prices that reduces the purchasing power of money.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation affects demand, business costs, and pricing strategy.

terms.definition: The fund a reseller earns at a stated rate on its purchases — say 3 percent of net purchases, so $400,000 bought builds a $12,000 balance — against which the supplier reimburses an agreed share, often 50 percent, of documented advertising cost up to that balance. Unspent accruals usually expire at year end, and claims without tear sheets or invoices are denied.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-and-promotion coordination roleplays ask how to fund a dealer's local campaign; the scored answer works from the accrued balance and the proof-of-performance requirement.

terms.definition: A prize promotion decided by judged ability — an essay, a photo, a recipe — rather than by random draw, which removes the chance element of an illegal lottery and is the only reason it may lawfully require a purchase, where a chance-based sweepstakes must offer free entry instead.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay client insists that entrants buy something first, this is the structure that makes it legal, and knowing which element each format removes is what turns a vague warning into usable advice.

terms.definition: The share of units clearing a step with no rework or scrap; multiplied across steps it gives rolled throughput yield, so four stations each at 95% deliver only 0.95^4 = 81.5% clean units, meaning a line whose every station reports 95% is really losing almost one unit in five.
terms.whyItMatters: Quality roleplays are scored on catching hidden rework: each station passing its own target while the finished-goods number falls short is exactly the scenario this calculation explains.

terms.definition: A review of a business's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats.
terms.whyItMatters: SWOT gives a structured frame for the situation analysis behind a plan.

terms.definition: Asking for the order or finalizing the agreement to complete the sale.
terms.whyItMatters: Knowing when and how to close prevents lost opportunities.

terms.definition: Nominal GDP divided by real GDP, times 100 — a price index covering every good and service an economy produces. Unlike the consumer price index it uses no fixed basket, so its weights shift automatically as spending patterns change, and it excludes imported goods that the CPI includes.
terms.whyItMatters: An item giving nominal and real GDP for the same year is asking for this ratio, and an item asking which price measure covers the whole economy rather than a household basket is asking for it by name.

terms.definition: A deduction a retailer subtracts from a supplier's invoice for breaking routing, labeling, carton or ship-window rules — typically $50 to $500 per occurrence, or 1 to 5 percent of the purchase-order value — netted out before payment rather than billed separately. Because it lands after the price is agreed, a supplier quoting an acceptable margin can still realize several points less on the account.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-profitability roleplays ask why a large account earns less than the price sheet implies; the deductions, not the negotiated price, are usually the answer.

terms.definition: An exclusive right granted by government to protect a new, useful invention.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors must recognize what innovations a business can legally protect from copying.

terms.definition: The same offering varies by employee, by customer, and by hour, so quality is a distribution rather than a specification; a factory good is held to a stated tolerance and any unit outside it is scrapped, while service variance has to be squeezed by scripts, training, and blueprints.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on internal service standards is scored on how you narrow the spread between your best and worst shift, not on restating that people differ.

terms.definition: A weighted score for ranking candidate countries or segments: each factor gets a weight, the weights sum to 1.0, each market gets a rating, and weight times rating summed gives one comparable number — so a market that scores well on a 0.10 factor still loses to one that scores well on a 0.40 factor.
terms.whyItMatters: Expansion cases hand over a table of markets and ask which to enter first; the defensible answer weights the criteria before scoring rather than counting how many boxes each market ticks.

terms.definition: The Federal Trade Commission provision giving a buyer until midnight of the third business day to cancel a sale of $25 or more made at their home or anywhere other than the seller's permanent place of business, with the seller required to hand over two dated cancellation forms at signing. Sales made inside the seller's own store are not covered.
terms.whyItMatters: Legal and ethical selling items on the exam test the dollar threshold and the location condition, and in-home roleplays expect you to disclose the cancellation right rather than hurry the signature.

terms.definition: The short-run inverse trade-off between inflation and unemployment: driving unemployment below the natural rate buys fewer jobless at the price of faster inflation. The long-run version is vertical at the natural rate, so once workers build the higher inflation into their expectations the trade-off disappears and only the inflation remains.
terms.whyItMatters: Items ask what a central bank gives up when it stimulates an economy already at full employment; the long-run vertical version is what explains why the 1970s tried to buy jobs and got stagflation instead.

terms.definition: Units sold to shoppers divided by units received, times 100, over a stated period: a store that took in 400 units and sold 260 in four weeks is at 65 percent. It is measured against sell-in, which counts only what the supplier shipped INTO the retailer — a supplier can post a record sell-in quarter while the goods sit unsold in the store, which is how channel stuffing hides itself.
terms.whyItMatters: Channel-performance roleplays give shipment figures and ask whether the launch is working; answering from sell-in instead of sell-through is the error judges are watching for.

terms.definition: Letter layout that keeps the inside address, salutation, body paragraphs and any lists flush at the left margin but starts the dateline, complimentary close and signature block at the horizontal center of the page - about the 3-inch tab on a page with 1-inch margins. That one shifted column is the only difference from full block; adding a half-inch first-line indent to every paragraph converts it again into semi-block.
terms.whyItMatters: Formatting questions show the same letter three ways and score the competitor who can point to which elements moved, rather than judging the page by how balanced it looks.

terms.definition: Sorts features into must-be, whose absence angers buyers while its presence earns nothing, performance features, where satisfaction rises with the amount delivered, and delighters, unnoticed when missing but thrilling when present -- and it predicts each delighter decays into a must-be as rivals copy it.
terms.whyItMatters: Feature-prioritization roleplays are scored on where to spend: pouring money into a must-be buys no preference, while the delighter that differentiates today becomes table stakes next season.

terms.definition: Dividing a market into distinct groups of customers with similar needs.
terms.whyItMatters: Segmentation lets a business target specific customer groups effectively.

terms.definition: Recommending additional products based on the customer's current purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Suggestive selling raises transaction value and meets more needs.

terms.definition: The percentage of the labor force actively seeking work but unable to find it.
terms.whyItMatters: It signals economic health and shapes consumer spending and hiring.

terms.definition: The chain of markups that turns factory cost into shelf price, each level pricing off ITS OWN selling price: $12 factory cost sold to a distributor working on a 20 percent margin becomes $15 ($12 / 0.80), and that $15 sold to a retailer working on a 40 percent margin becomes $25 ($15 / 0.60). Dividing by one minus the margin is the step students miss when they add the percentages instead.
terms.whyItMatters: Pricing-and-channel roleplays ask what a product must leave the factory at to hit a $25 shelf price; you have to work the stack backwards through every level's margin.

terms.definition: One question rated 1 to 7 on how easy the company made it to get an issue resolved, scored either as the share answering 5 to 7 or as a plain mean. It is asked right after a single service interaction rather than about the relationship, and it predicts repeat purchase better than satisfaction does, because removing effort keeps customers while delight rarely moves them.
terms.whyItMatters: In a service-redesign roleplay, arguing for deleting steps rather than adding perks needs this metric to carry the recommendation.

terms.definition: A process map drawn in horizontal bands split by the line of interaction, the line of visibility, and the line of internal interaction, so front-stage steps the customer sees sit above the backstage support that produces them, with failure points and wait times marked on the flow.
terms.whyItMatters: Operations roleplays that ask you to redesign a guest experience are scored on separating what the customer sees from the support behind it, which is where most delays actually live.

terms.definition: (area population x annual category spending per person) / total retail selling space devoted to that category — dollars of demand per square foot of supply. A high result means demand outruns the space serving it and the trade area can carry another store; a low one means the area is already saturated.
terms.whyItMatters: Retail expansion cases hand over population, per-person spending and competitors' square footage, and the expected recommendation follows from computing this ratio rather than counting rival stores.

terms.definition: Exaggerated subjective praise no reasonable buyer would treat as fact — the finest coffee in town — which creates no liability, as opposed to a misrepresentation, a specific factual claim about performance, condition or origin that does. The dividing test is whether the statement could be proven false.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethical selling roleplays plant a tempting overstatement, and knowing that this machine will cut your costs in half is a checkable claim while our machines are the best is not keeps you on the right side of the rubric.

terms.definition: The empirical rule that each percentage point of unemployment above the natural rate costs roughly 2% of potential real GDP, so an economy running 3 points above that rate is producing about 6% less than its capacity.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that give an actual unemployment rate and a natural rate and ask what output is being lost are solved with this two-to-one ratio rather than by describing the recession in words.

terms.definition: The supplier's own driver delivers to the individual store and often stocks the shelf, so the retailer never takes possession at a warehouse and title passes at the store door. Warehouse delivery is the alternative: the retailer receives at its own distribution center, takes title there, and self-distributes — cheaper per case, but adding days of lag that short-shelf-life and high-turn items cannot absorb.
terms.whyItMatters: Beverage, snack and bakery channel scenarios test which method fits a perishable line and who therefore controls the shelf set and out-of-stock recovery.

terms.definition: Blaming an out-group's failures on what its members are like while writing off its successes as luck, special help or an exception -- and reversing both judgments for one's own group. The individual-level attribution error concerns one person; this is its group-level extension, and it is the specific mechanism by which a stereotype survives meeting a counterexample, since the counterexample gets filed away rather than counted.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items on overcoming stereotypes reward naming the filing-as-exception move, and a Human Resources roleplay about a hiring panel that keeps calling qualified candidates from one school 'unusual for their program' is describing this error rather than open prejudice.

terms.definition: The matrix that converts weighted customer wants into engineering specifications, scoring each intersection 9, 3, or 1 for a strong, moderate, or weak relationship, then ranking every specification by the sum of customer weight times relationship score to decide what engineering works on first.
terms.whyItMatters: A product-development roleplay that must justify which feature ships first is scored on tracing the choice back to weighted customer input rather than to engineering preference.

terms.definition: Forecast accuracy scored as the average of |actual minus forecast| / actual across periods — a +10% miss and a -10% miss do not cancel, because the absolute value is taken before averaging. That is exactly what separates it from forecast bias, which keeps the signs.
terms.whyItMatters: Sales-forecasting items give several months of forecast and actual pairs and ask how accurate the method was; averaging the signed errors returns a flattering near-zero that the item is designed to catch.

terms.definition: A seller's factual affirmation, description, sample or model that becomes part of the basis of the bargain, created by the statement itself with no formal words and no intent required — where an implied warranty arises automatically from the sale by operation of law. A rep quoting a performance figure in a presentation can create one without meaning to.
terms.whyItMatters: Selling exam items ask which of four salesperson statements creates a binding promise, and the answer is always the specific, checkable one rather than the general praise beside it.

terms.definition: The labor force — everyone employed or actively searching within the last four weeks — divided by the civilian noninstitutional population aged 16 and over, times 100. It can fall at the same time as the unemployment rate, because a discouraged worker who stops searching leaves the numerator and the jobless count simultaneously.
terms.whyItMatters: Items pair a falling unemployment rate with a falling participation rate and ask whether the labor market really improved; the arithmetic of who leaves the labor force is what settles it.

terms.definition: Goods placed with a reseller while the SUPPLIER keeps title until the item sells: the reseller pays only for what it sells and returns the rest, so obsolescence and markdown risk stay upstream. To keep the stock out of the reseller's bankruptcy estate the supplier must file a UCC-1 financing statement under UCC Article 9, section 9-319 — without it, a court can treat the goods as the reseller's own.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay pitching an untested product to a cautious retailer is scored on offering this structure and on naming what the supplier gives up in exchange for the placement.

terms.definition: A financial statement showing revenue, expenses, and profit over a period of time.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the primary tool for judging whether operations are profitable.

terms.definition: The element of a brand that is recognized but cannot be spoken -- a symbol, distinctive lettering, color, or design -- as against the brand name, which is the part said aloud, and the trade name, which identifies the company rather than any product it sells.
terms.whyItMatters: Brand-building roleplays are scored on naming the pieces separately, since a logo redesign and a name change are different decisions with different legal and equity consequences.

terms.definition: A projection of expected future sales based on analysis and historical data.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecasts help plan resources and set realistic marketing objectives.

terms.definition: Developing a base of regular customers who return to buy again.
terms.whyItMatters: A strong clientele provides stable revenue and drives growth.

terms.definition: The ability to produce a good at a lower OPPORTUNITY cost than a trading partner, which is what makes trade mutually profitable even when one country is more efficient at producing everything. Absolute advantage — simply making more per hour of input — does not by itself establish any reason to trade.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade items give a two-country, two-good output table and ask who should specialize in what; the answer comes from the opportunity-cost ratios, not from whichever column of raw output is larger.

terms.definition: A partner-program rule granting the FIRST partner to register a named end-customer opportunity an exclusive extra discount — commonly 5 to 20 points below standard partner price — for a fixed window of about 60 to 90 days. It exists to stop two partners quoting the same customer and bidding the vendor's own product down, and it lapses automatically if the window closes without a sale.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-to-business channel roleplays about two resellers chasing one account are graded on this mechanism, which resolves the conflict without the vendor picking a favorite.

terms.definition: The degree of discretionary effort and psychological commitment a worker brings to the organization's goals, measured through driver surveys covering manager quality, recognition and growth. It is not job satisfaction: a comfortable employee can be entirely satisfied and contribute nothing extra, which is why engagement tracks against productivity and turnover while satisfaction alone often does not.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking how to build stronger employer-employee relationships expects engagement drivers and a measurement plan rather than a morale-boosting event.

terms.definition: A standard states the minimum a unit must meet to be sold under a name at all, while a grade ranks the units that already clear it -- USDA beef sorted Prime, Choice, or Select by marbling and maturity has met one identical wholesomeness standard at every grade.
terms.whyItMatters: Buying and menu roleplays are scored on specifying the grade you will purchase; saying a product 'meets standards' says nothing about the quality tier you promised the customer.

terms.definition: Next period's forecast equals alpha times this period's actual plus (1 minus alpha) times this period's forecast, with alpha between 0 and 1. A high alpha makes the forecast chase recent movement; a low alpha holds it steady, and every past period stays in the number at a shrinking weight.
terms.whyItMatters: Forecasting questions give last period's forecast, its actual and a smoothing constant and expect one number back; they also ask which alpha suits a volatile category, which is a judgment the formula makes visible.

terms.definition: Share of one cohort of leads that becomes a qualified opportunity: opportunities created divided by the leads that entered in that same period, never by every lead sitting in the database. 40 opportunities from 500 new leads is 8 percent; dividing by a 12,000-record database reports 0.3 percent and hides the follow-up problem entirely.
terms.whyItMatters: Funnel-math items hand you a month of lead counts and opportunity counts and grade the denominator you pick, and a roleplay on tracking prospecting results expects the rate quoted per period rather than against the whole list.

terms.definition: The total market value of all final goods and services a country produces in a year.
terms.whyItMatters: GDP is the standard gauge of economic health competitors reference.

terms.definition: The EDI 856 document a supplier transmits BEFORE the truck arrives, listing carton-level contents keyed to SSCC-18 pallet labels so the receiver scans the shipment in instead of counting units. It is the mirror of the EDI 850 purchase order, which OPENS the transaction by stating what the buyer wants; the 856 closes the loop by declaring what is actually on the way, and a late or inaccurate one is the most common chargeback trigger.
terms.whyItMatters: Technology-in-channel-management questions test whether you can name which transaction set does what between trading partners, not merely that they exchange data electronically.

terms.definition: The European rule granting individuals rights of access, correction, portability and erasure over their own data, requiring a documented lawful basis before any processing begins, forcing breach notification to the supervisory authority within 72 hours, and capping fines at the greater of 20 million euros or 4% of worldwide annual turnover.
terms.whyItMatters: An international e-commerce roleplay asks what changes when the site starts shipping to Ireland, and the answer is these specific obligations and their clock, not a general promise of privacy.

terms.definition: Loss of trademark rights when the public adopts a mark as the common name for the whole product class -- aspirin, escalator, thermos; the Lanham Act's Section 14(3) test is the mark's primary significance to the relevant public, so an owner's protests do not save it once ordinary usage has flipped.
terms.whyItMatters: Branding roleplays about protecting a name are scored on naming the concrete defenses -- always pairing the mark with the generic noun, policing verb use -- and on why success itself creates the risk.

terms.definition: Among households that buy the brand at all, the percentage of their category purchases it captures. A brand bought by 20% of households that supplies 60% of those households' category volume has 60% share of requirements but only 12% market share (0.20 x 0.60).
terms.whyItMatters: Growth-diagnosis items ask whether a brand should recruit new buyers or deepen existing ones; a high requirements share with low penetration points to recruitment, and the two numbers must be read together.

terms.definition: The emotional and rational reasons a customer makes a purchase.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding motives helps position products around what matters.

terms.definition: The complete record of a nation's transactions with the rest of the world — the current account of goods, services, income and transfers, plus the capital and financial accounts — which sums to zero by construction, since a current-account deficit is financed by an offsetting inflow of capital. The balance of trade is only the goods-and-services slice of the current account.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-business items ask what a persistent trade deficit implies; the correct answer follows the offsetting capital inflow rather than treating the deficit as unfunded loss.

terms.definition: A facility built to pick individual EACHES and ship parcels to consumers, so it is staffed for pick-pack labor, carries returns processing, and is measured in orders per hour. A distribution center serves STORES instead: it moves full cases and pallets on scheduled truck routes, needs far less labor per unit, and is measured in cases shipped.
terms.whyItMatters: E-commerce channel roleplays ask why store-serving warehouses cannot simply absorb online orders; the unit of work and the labor cost per unit are the scored distinction.

terms.definition: Optimizes the discounted value of a customer's entire future stream of purchases and will accept a thinner margin on any single sale to protect it, whereas transactional marketing maximizes margin on each separate exchange and budgets acquisition and retention as unrelated lines; the two approaches give opposite answers to whether a long-standing customer should be granted a concession on one order.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay in which a loyal customer asks for an exception is decided by which of the two frames you argue from, and judges expect the alternative named.

terms.definition: Planning, developing, marketing, and managing offerings across their life.
terms.whyItMatters: It ensures offerings meet customer needs and generate sustainable revenue.

terms.definition: A specific, measurable goal for what marketing should achieve.
terms.whyItMatters: Clear objectives keep strategies and tactics aligned with business goals.

terms.definition: Total quota handed out across the sales force divided by the revenue the company actually forecasts. Assigning 1.1 to 1.3 times the target is deliberate over-assignment that absorbs ramping reps, mid-year attrition and under-performers, so the plan still lands if some reps miss — it measures quota against target, where pipeline coverage measures open deals against quota.
terms.whyItMatters: A sales-management roleplay that asks you to set quotas for next year is scored on whether you over-assign on purpose and can say why; the exam pairs this with pipeline coverage to see if you can tell the two ratios apart.
